h: Burns, Mary and a Building Made for Faces
p: The gallery opened in 1889 in a building designed by Robert Rowand Anderson specifically to house portraits, making it the first purpose-built portrait gallery anywhere in the world. Its creation was largely paid for by John Ritchie Findlay, owner of The Scotsman newspaper. Before you go in, have a good look at the outside: the walls are studded with statues of famous Scots, a sort of hall of fame in sandstone.

Inside, there are a few portraits most people want to tick off. The famous image of Robert Burns painted by his friend Alexander Nasmyth is here, as are portraits of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Bonnie Prince Charlie. Spotting how artists flattered, or failed to flatter, their sitters is half the fun. The building had a big refurbishment that reopened it in 2011, so the galleries feel light and airy despite the Victorian setting.

Entry to the collection is free, though some special exhibitions can be charged. The tram stops at St Andrew Square, a couple of minutes away, and Edinburgh Bus Station is just round the corner too, which makes it a handy first or last stop. If you've got the bug afterwards, the Scottish National Gallery on the Mound is a short walk downhill and has old masters to keep you going.
